summary: Defines a TLS extension that lets a client say how many session tickets it wants from the server. Session tickets let a client resume a later connection without the server keeping per-client state. Letting the client ask for a number helps servers avoid issuing wasted tickets while still giving clients enough for future connections.

plainLanguage.summary: When you borrow tickets for a ride, you tell the clerk how many you need, so none are wasted and you do not run out.

subtitle: A TLS extension that lets a client tell the server how many session tickets it wants.

tldr.problem: TLS servers hand out some fixed number of session tickets per connection, and clients have no way to say how many they actually need, which leads to ticket reuse or wasted tickets.
tldr.mechanism: A client adds a ticket_request extension to its ClientHello with two counts, one for a new session and one for a resumption. The server treats them as hints and answers with an expected_count in EncryptedExtensions.
tldr.outcome: Servers can issue about as many tickets as clients need and no more, and clients can keep enough tickets for parallel or racing connections. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9149 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the ticket_request extension.

sections.title: Why Ticket Counts Need a Say
sections.content:
In TLS 1.3, a server sends session tickets in NewSessionTicket messages so a client can resume a later connection without the server keeping per-client state. The server decides how many to send. RFC 8446 leaves that choice to the server, and RFC 9149 names three limits of that design.

  • Servers often send a hard-coded number, and no static number suits every situation.
  • Clients cannot say how many tickets they want. A client that opens parallel connections or races connections across interfaces needs several tickets to avoid reusing one.
  • All tickets derive from an initial connection. If a server forces a fresh connection, the other tickets from that session may also be invalid, so the client may need a larger batch to refill its cache.
sections.plainLanguage: A shop hands out the same number of coupons to everyone, even if you need more or fewer. This lets you say how many you want.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC lists four reasons to ask for a specific number of tickets.

  • Parallel HTTP connections: a client can use a distinct ticket on each connection. It must bound its parallel connections by the tickets it holds, or risk ticket reuse.
  • Connection racing: techniques such as Happy Eyeballs V2 (RFC 8305) race attempts across interfaces and address families. Separate tickets avoid reuse and keep the cache from emptying. Some servers use single-use tickets, so distinct tickets also stop racing from invalidating them early.
  • Less ticket waste: moving the count decision to clients means servers do not generate unneeded tickets. Ticket generation can involve expensive computation such as public key operations.
  • Decline resumption: a client can send a count of zero to show it does not intend to resume.
sections.plainLanguage: If you and your friends all go through the gate at the same moment, each of you needs your own ticket. If you are not coming back, you can say you need none.

sections.title: The ticket_request Extension
sections.content:
Clients MAY send a ticket_request extension (extension type 58) in the ClientHello. It holds a ClientTicketRequest structure with two uint8 fields.

  • new_session_count: tickets wanted if the server negotiates a new connection.
  • resumption_count: tickets wanted if the server resumes using a ticket presented in this ClientHello.

A server that supports and uses the extension MUST also send ticket_request in EncryptedExtensions. That copy carries a ServerTicketRequestHint with one uint8 field, expected_count, the number of tickets the server expects to send on this connection.

The extension applies to TLS 1.3, DTLS 1.3 (RFC 9147) and future versions of (D)TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The client writes two numbers on a note: how many tickets for a first visit and how many for a return visit. The server writes back how many it plans to give.

sections.title: How Clients and Servers Use the Counts
sections.content:
A client starting a new connection SHOULD set new_session_count to the number of tickets it wants and resumption_count to 0. Once its cache is primed, a resumption_count of 1 lets the server replace each ticket with a new one without over-provisioning. A client that races several connections, each with its own ticket, would end up with tickets from only one resumed session, so it can send a resumption_count equal to the number of parallel attempts. A smaller count might leave it with zero tickets.

If a client presents a ticket and the server still negotiates a new connection, the client SHOULD assume the other tickets from the same session are no longer valid for resumption.

Servers SHOULD NOT send more tickets than requested for the connection type they chose, and SHOULD cap the number they are willing to send. The count is typically the minimum of the server's own limit and the request. A server MAY send more later if the original tickets are invalidated.

Servers MUST NOT send ticket_request in any other handshake message, including ServerHello or HelloRetryRequest. A client MUST abort with an illegal_parameter alert if it sees one. After a HelloRetryRequest, the second ClientHello MUST keep the extension present or absent as before and MUST NOT change its value.
sections.plainLanguage: The server treats your note as a polite request. It will not give you more than you asked for, and it keeps its own limit too.

sections.title: Performance Considerations
sections.content: Servers can send tickets any time after the server Finished message. Sending many tickets before application data can hurt performance. For example, on a connection with a constrained congestion window, ticket messages could delay application data. The RFC advises servers to prioritize application data over tickets when possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not hand out a pile of tickets before the show starts if that makes the show start late. Show first, tickets after.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Ticket reuse is a security and privacy concern, and clients pooling tickets must be careful. If servers do not rotate ticket encryption keys often, clients may keep tickets beyond common lifetimes such as 24 hours. Clients SHOULD discard cached tickets after a reasonable time that mimics the key rotation period, and MUST NOT cache tickets for longer than 7 days.

If a server sends tickets right after its Finished message without verifying the client's IP address, for example with the TLS cookie extension, an attacker can use spoofed UDP packets in a (D)TLS key exchange to cause an amplification attack proportional to the count. Servers SHOULD limit tickets until they have verified the address.

Servers with no limit on tickets sent in response to ticket_request may be open to denial-of-service attacks, especially if ticket creation is expensive.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not let someone ask for a giant stack of tickets, and throw away old tickets so nobody can use them long after they were given out.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA added ticket_request to the "TLS ExtensionType Values" registry with value 58. It is marked for TLS 1.3 in CH (ClientHello) and EE (EncryptedExtensions), as not DTLS-only, and as recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension got its own official number, 58, in the big list of TLS extensions.
